title: A sundew leaf can fold right over its prey, bending more than 180 degrees

cover.alt: A long, straight Cape sundew leaf covered in red hairs tipped with glistening droplets.

body: Each leaf of the Cape sundew, *Drosera capensis*, a carnivorous plant from South Africa, is covered in stalked glands that ooze droplets of sticky mucilage laced with digestive enzymes. An insect that lands gets stuck. Then the leaf itself slowly bends in around the spot where the prey is held, enfolding it. In this species the leaf can bend **more than 180°**, rolling right around its catch.

slides.alt: A long, red-haired sundew leaf with a fruit fly stuck to it slowly bends in the middle until its tip folds back over the catch.
slides.caption: Time-lapse of a Cape sundew leaf after catching a fruit fly: about 4 hours in 16 seconds, as the leaf slowly bends and folds over its prey.

steps.label: Sticky droplets trap a landing insect
The leaf slowly bends around it
Enzymes in the mucilage digest it

slides.question: Fresh Cape sundew glue is very stringy. How long a thread can it pull out into?
slides.explanation: When fresh, the mucilage is so sticky that it can be drawn out into threads up to 1 m long.

slides.text: …at this present moment I care more about Drosera than the origin of all the species in the world.
slides.attribution: Charles Darwin on sundews, letter to Charles Lyell, 24 November 1860

slides.heading: Easy to grow, easy to watch
slides.text: The Cape sundew is one of the easiest carnivorous plants to keep: it is simple to propagate, grows fast and flowers readily, with pale purple flowers that open one after another up a tall stalk.
